turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry I'm late, doctor. The number 19 sat behind a bin lorry and then I came in the wrong door.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're fine, Mr Hale. Have a seat. Were you rushing?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit. I was up the allotment at half six staking beans, and next door's cat was in the compost again. Filthy animal.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Quite a start. What did you come in for, though?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Ah. Right. It's the waterworks. I'm up three or four times a night for a wee, the stream's gone weak, and I dribble after.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): So night-time trips, a poor stream, and dribbling at the end.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. I stand there and it just trickles. Takes forever, and then there's a little bit more in the pants.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Err, did I even lock the shed. I keep seeing that fork left out in the rain, and if it rusts...
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry. Umm, I couldn't put a date on it, it's been months but it crept up, and I really don't know when it started.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. No clear start, then. Is the dribbling the same, or newer?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): The dribbling's the newer bit. Last few weeks. The getting up and the weak stream, that's the one that's been months.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the urine?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): Blood? God no. My brother, he had a thing with his...
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stay with you a second, sorry. No blood that you've actually seen?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): None. Not once. I would have noticed, I'm sure.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Burning or pain when you pass water?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No burning, no pain. It's just slow.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Through the day, are you rushing, or is it mainly the nights?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Mainly the nights. I do go more in the day than I used to, but I'm not dashing for it.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you drinking in the evening?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Tea. Always a pot while the news is on, 2 or 3 mugs, and another if the football's on. Can't drop the evening brew.

[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): That late fluid will keep waking you. It isn't the whole reason for a weak stream, but it piles on the night trips. Think of the bladder as a tank you're topping up at bedtime.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): I did wonder. My dad was the same, ended up having the prostate out when he was about seventy. I sit there at night and I think of him.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's worth knowing, thank you. Medicines, what are you on just now?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Ramipril. Five milligrams, mornings, for the blood pressure. Been on it years. Nothing else, uh, far as I remember.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ever had a PSA, the prostate blood test?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): They did one at the hospital, three-ish years ago. They said it was borderline. I never got a number, and nobody chased me, so I let it lie.

[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Borderline, and no figure. Alright. Thinking it through, weak stream, dribbling, up at night, in a chap your age, this is most likely the prostate enlarging in the ordinary benign way.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't properly exclude a cancer from the story alone, so I don't want to call it that, but it isn't what the pattern is shouting.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): That's the bit I didn't want to say out loud. The cancer word.

[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Understood. What I am going to do is book a PSA blood test and a urine sample, today. The urine is to look for blood we haven't seen and for infection. The PSA is the fresh prostate check.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Do I fill the pot here?
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, before you go, if you can. Reception will hand you the bottle. I'll put both requests in now, so they're arranged, not a maybe.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): And if the PSA's up?
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then we talk about what it means. It isn't a diagnosis on its own. There's also a tablet I want to start, called tamsulosin.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Never heard of it.

[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Four hundred micrograms, one capsule by mouth at night. It eases the muscle at the neck of the bladder so the stream often picks up. First few doses can make you light-headed if you stand up fast, more so with ramipril on board, so take it once you're in for the night.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Tamsolosin, right. Will it fight with the ramipril?

[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tamsulosin. Not a fight, but both can drop the pressure a little, so if you feel faint you sit down and you tell me. I'd like you on it starting tonight if the chemist has it. I'll send the prescription.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Alright. I'll try it. Nights are grim enough already.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): And ease off that evening tea. Half a mug, earlier if you can. Don't stop the ramipril.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Half a mug. The football will feel all wrong, but fine.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bowels been alright, any change?
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): Bowels are fine. Clockwork. Sorry, I do rattle on about nothing.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're alright. I've felt your tummy, it's soft, and I can't feel the bladder. I'm leaving the prostate examination today, the blood test is the useful bit first.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): Soft is good, is it?
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): It is. Come back and see me in about four weeks, results in hand, and we'll see if the tamsulosin suits you. Put it on the calendar so it doesn't drift.

spec.situation: Older man getting up three to four times at night, weak stream, dribbling; drinks tea in the evening; denies blood in urine; PSA and urine tests planned, tamsulosin discussed.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

bad.reason: Patient says not dashing for it, but urgency was not directly assessed or denied.
Prior PSA was completed, but it was three-ish years ago at hospital, not current completed test.

omissions.text: Family history was more specific than 'prostate problems': the patient's father had his prostate removed at about age 70.

Previous PSA was done at hospital about three years ago and was described to the patient as 'borderline'; he was not given the value and no one followed it up. The recorded completed PSA entry lacks these details.

Daytime urinary frequency was qualified as mild: he goes more in the day than he used to, but is 'not dashing for it' and it is mainly a night-time problem. Recording this as urinary urgency absent is wrong because urgency was not asked about directly.
The doctor advised the urine sample should be provided before the patient leaves, with reception handing him the bottle, and said both requests would be put in now so they were definitely arranged.
Tamsulosin counselling included that the first few doses can make him light-headed specifically when standing up quickly, and that this risk is greater because he is also taking ramipril.
The doctor advised starting tamsulosin tonight if the chemist has it and said he would send the prescription.
Advice on fluids was more specific: reduce evening tea to half a mug and have it earlier if possible.
Follow-up was specified as coming back in about four weeks with the results available/in hand, to review both the results and whether tamsulosin suits him.
